questions.article: In Singapore, the Enraged Go to the Fragment Room
questions.q: The editorial describes “rage rooms” where people smash things to relieve stress. What does it recommend instead when one is angry?
options: Tell everyone how you feel
Not quite. The article says: Stay completely silent and carry on with positive work, so the energy of anger feeds creativity.
Stay completely silent and carry on with positive work, so the energy of anger feeds creativity
Yes. Anger is “a great natural gift” to be used wisely.
Take a long holiday at once
Not quite. The article says: Stay completely silent and carry on with positive work, so the energy of anger feeds creativity.
Shout in a place where no one can hear
Not quite. The article says: Stay completely silent and carry on with positive work, so the energy of anger feeds creativity.
questions.rationale: “All you need to do when you get angry is to keep mum. Your total silence will automatically initiate a natural process within you and the released ‘anger energy’ will be diverted to a positive target.”

questions.q: Milk does not exist ready-made in a cow; it is produced by an inner process. What point about spirituality does this make?
options: It is found only in beautiful places
Not quite. The article says: It is not found ready-made outside – a prepared, thinking mind must produce it from its experiences.
It comes without any effort
Not quite. The article says: It is not found ready-made outside – a prepared, thinking mind must produce it from its experiences.
It is not found ready-made outside – a prepared, thinking mind must produce it from its experiences
Right. “A product of your own factory.”
It can be bought from an expert
Not quite. The article says: It is not found ready-made outside – a prepared, thinking mind must produce it from its experiences.
questions.rationale: “Spirituality is not a ready-made thing. It is a product of an intellectual process… Rather you must develop your own mind and soul.”

questions.q: The umbrella and the hand pump once caused amazement and are now ordinary. What lesson does the article draw?
options: New inventions are soon replaced
Not quite. The article says: Familiarity dulls wonder – we should look at God’s creation as if seeing it for the first time.
People were once easily fooled
Not quite. The article says: Familiarity dulls wonder – we should look at God’s creation as if seeing it for the first time.
Old things were better made
Not quite. The article says: Familiarity dulls wonder – we should look at God’s creation as if seeing it for the first time.
Familiarity dulls wonder – we should look at God’s creation as if seeing it for the first time
Well read. Like one cured of blindness.
questions.rationale: “We should not lose our sense of awe and gratitude simply because familiarity has taken the edge off our awareness.”

questions.q: Ali was asked whether he had any inspiration beyond the Quran. What did his answer show?
options: That he possessed secret writings
Not quite. The article says: Reading the words is one thing; grasping the deeper meaning needs reflection and God-given understanding.
That only Arabic speakers can benefit from the Quran
Not quite. The article says: Reading the words is one thing; grasping the deeper meaning needs reflection and God-given understanding.
That the Quran need only be recited
Not quite. The article says: Reading the words is one thing; grasping the deeper meaning needs reflection and God-given understanding.
Reading the words is one thing; grasping the deeper meaning needs reflection and God-given understanding
Yes. The Quran is an ocean to be explored in depth.
questions.rationale: “To understand the words of the Quran all one has to do is read it. But true understanding of Quranic meanings can only come from deep thought and contemplation.”

questions.q: Which experiences does the article call the real “test papers” of life?
options: Routine daily tasks
Not quite. The article says: Situations demanding a moral choice, especially dilemmas where the right course is hard to see.
Situations demanding a moral choice, especially dilemmas where the right course is hard to see
Correct. Routine matters test nothing.
School and college examinations
Not quite. The article says: Situations demanding a moral choice, especially dilemmas where the right course is hard to see.
Contests with other people
Not quite. The article says: Situations demanding a moral choice, especially dilemmas where the right course is hard to see.
questions.rationale: “Some other types of experience… place us in the dilemma of not being able to tell which the right course is… It is such experiences which are the real ‘test papers’ in life.”

questions.q: If a person finds himself in rank and affluence, what does the article say he must guard against?
options: Arrogance, pride and miserliness
Right. As poverty calls for patience and gratitude.
Too much generosity
Not quite. The article says: Arrogance, pride and miserliness.
Idleness and boredom
Not quite. The article says: Arrogance, pride and miserliness.
Impatience and despair
Not quite. The article says: Arrogance, pride and miserliness.
questions.rationale: “One may… find oneself in a position of rank and affluence, in which case it is arrogance, overweening pride and miserliness which have to be guarded against.”

questions.q: Mr Khan was appointed almost without an interview because his former professor already knew his work. What moral does the article draw?
options: Make yourself genuinely useful and able, and opportunities will seek you out
Well reasoned. The world runs on give and take.
Interviews serve no purpose
Not quite. The article says: Make yourself genuinely useful and able, and opportunities will seek you out.
Good connections matter more than merit
Not quite. The article says: Make yourself genuinely useful and able, and opportunities will seek you out.
Private colleges choose carelessly
Not quite. The article says: Make yourself genuinely useful and able, and opportunities will seek you out.
questions.rationale: “If you want employment, you must make yourself useful… Then you will see that you don’t need to pursue employment instead employment will pursue you.”

questions.q: Man longs for a perfect world but lives in an imperfect, passing one. What does the article reason from this?
options: The world was once perfect and has declined
Not quite. The article says: Another, perfect and lasting world must follow; this one is a place of trial.
Man’s longing is a mere illusion
Not quite. The article says: Another, perfect and lasting world must follow; this one is a place of trial.
Another, perfect and lasting world must follow; this one is a place of trial
Yes. So one should not try to build heaven on earth.
Perfection can be reached here with effort
Not quite. The article says: Another, perfect and lasting world must follow; this one is a place of trial.
questions.rationale: “This world must be inconclusive. Another world must follow to compensate for the inadequacies of the present one.”

questions.q: When armed tribes reached the borders of Madinah at the time of Al-Ahzab, what did the Prophet and his Companions do?
options: Left the city by night
Not quite. The article says: Dug a trench, which prevented a battle from taking place.
Sent for help from distant allies
Not quite. The article says: Dug a trench, which prevented a battle from taking place.
Dug a trench, which prevented a battle from taking place
Right. An example of averting war.
Marched out to meet them in the open
Not quite. The article says: Dug a trench, which prevented a battle from taking place.
questions.rationale: “The Prophet and his Companions dug a deep trench between them, thus successfully preventing a battle from taking place.”

questions.q: “Be an idealist in your own home, and as soon as you step out of your home, become practical.” What does this mean?
options: Expect the highest of yourself, but only what is realistically possible of others
Exactly. Doing the opposite leads to failure.
Keep your ideals private
Not quite. The article says: Expect the highest of yourself, but only what is realistically possible of others.
Be strict with family and easy with strangers
Not quite. The article says: Expect the highest of yourself, but only what is realistically possible of others.
Dream at home and work outside
Not quite. The article says: Expect the highest of yourself, but only what is realistically possible of others.
questions.rationale: “We need to be realist when it comes to others and idealist when it comes to our own selves.”
